o: Letters map to digits by QWERTY keyboard position (qwertyuiop→1..10, asdfghjkl→11..19, zxcvbnm→20..26). A substring is divisible if its mapped sum divides evenly by its length. With n <= 2000, counting all O(n²) substrings with a running sum is perfectly fine — example "asdf" yields 6 divisible substrings.
k: Mapping is positional on the QWERTY layout, not alphabetical.
Running sums make each substring's mapped sum O(1) to obtain.

a.n: Approach 1: Running-sum enumeration of all substrings
a.i: Fix the left endpoint i, extend j while adding the mapped digit; check divisibility at each step. All single characters are automatically divisible (digit divides itself), matching the examples.
s: Build the digit map from the QWERTY string.
For each i, accumulate sum over j >= i.
a.t: O(n²) — every substring visited once with O(1) work.
a.sp: O(1) extra space beyond the 26-entry map.

w: Simple problem; the only trap is assuming alphabetical mapping — verify with the given table ('a'=1 but 's'=7). A follow-up could raise n to 1e5, requiring per-length modular prefix counting (fix length L, count prefix sums ≡ 0 mod L via buckets) for O(n·√S) overall.
